Study the given graph and answer the question that follows.

The graph shows the data of production of items: W, R and T by four companies: S, D, F and G as percentage of their total production.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/b1e699b99f94bd5e3e2e3e402ae9dc1e320a474a3a3766940d147760ad7912a2.png] 

If the total productions of F and S are 2000 and 3000, respectively, the difference in the productions of R by these companies is:
questions.solution:
**Given:**

For Company F, the production of item R is 35% of its total production.

For Company S, the production of item R is 30% of its total production.

Total production of Company F = 2000

Total production of Company S = 3000

**Calculations:**

Production of R by F = 35% of Total production of F

Production of R by F = (35 ⁄ 100) × 2000

Production of R by F = 35 × 20 = 700

Production of R by S = 30% of Total production of S

Production of R by S = (30 ⁄ 100) × 3000

Production of R by S = 30 × 30 = 900

Difference = Production of R by S - Production of R by F

Difference = 900 - 700 = 200

**∴ The correct answer 
is 200.**

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells one-fourth of his items at a loss of 12%, one-third of the remaining items at a profit of 44%, and the rest at a loss of 7%. What is his overall profit/loss percentage?
questions.solution:
**Given:**

A shopkeeper sells:

One-fourth (1/4) of items at a loss of 12%

One-third (1/3) of the remaining items at a profit of 44%

Rest at a loss of 7%

**Formula used:**

Overall Profit/Loss (%) = dfrac{{Total Profit or Loss}}{{Total Cost Price}} times 100

**Calculation:**

Let total cost price (C.P.) of all items = ₹100.

One-fourth of items: dfrac{1}{4} times 100 = ₹25

Loss on these items = dfrac{12}{100} times 25 = ₹3

Remaining items: dfrac{3}{4} times 100 = ₹75

One-third of these remaining items: dfrac{1}{3} times 75 = ₹25

Profit on these items = dfrac{44}{100} times 25 = ₹11

Rest of the items: dfrac{2}{3} times 75 = ₹50

Loss on these items = dfrac{7}{100} times 50 = ₹3.5

Total Loss = ₹3 + ₹3.5 = ₹6.5

Total Profit = ₹11

Net Profit = Total Profit - Total Loss = ₹11 - ₹6.5 = ₹4.5

Overall Profit/Loss Percentage = dfrac{4.5}{100} times 100 = 4.5\%

**∴ The correct answer is option (2): 4.5% gain.**

questions.question: A thief Rohan is spotted by a policeman Ramesh from a distance of 250 m. When they see each other, they start running. How much distance is covered by Rohan, who is running at the speed of 20 km/h, before being caught by Ramesh, who is running at the speed of 25 km/h?
questions.solution:
**Given:**

Distance between Rohan and Ramesh = 250 m

Speed of Rohan = 20 km/h

Speed of Ramesh = 25 km/h

**Formula used:**

Relative speed = Speed of Ramesh - Speed of Rohan

Time taken to catch = Distance / Relative speed

Distance covered by Rohan = Time taken × Speed of Rohan

**Calculation:**

Relative speed = 25 - 20 = 5 km/h

Convert distance to km: 250 m = 0.25 km

Time taken = Distance / Relative speed

⇒ Time taken = 0.25 / 5 = 0.05 hours

Distance covered by Rohan = Time taken × Speed of Rohan

⇒ Distance covered = 0.05 × 20 = 1 km

**∴ The correct answer is option (3).**

questions.question: Find the greatest possible length which can be used to measure exactly the lengths 2 m 25 cm, 2 m 70 cm, 3 m 15 cm.
questions.solution:
**Given:**

Lengths to be measured are 2 m 25 cm, 2 m 70 cm, and 3 m 15 cm.

**Concept Used:**

To find the greatest possible length, we need to find the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of the three lengths.

**Calculation:**

All lengths to centimeters:

2 m 25 cm = (2 × 100) + 25 = 200 + 25 = 225 cm

2 m 70 cm = (2 × 100) + 70 = 200 + 70 = 270 cm

3 m 15 cm = (3 × 100) + 15 = 300 + 15 = 315 cm

⇒ Find the prime factors of each number:

225 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 3² × 5²

270 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2¹ × 3³ × 5¹

315 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 3² × 5¹ × 7¹

The greatest common divisor (GCD) by taking the lowest power of the common prime factors:

Common prime factors are 3 and 5.

Lowest power of 3 is 3².

Lowest power of 5 is 5¹.

GCD = 3² × 5¹ = 9 × 5 = 45 cm

**∴ The greatest possible length is 45 cm.**

questions.question: Who appointed the ‘Hunter Commission’ for Educational Reforms in 1882?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Ripon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Hunter Commission was appointed in **1882** by **Lord Ripon**, the then Viceroy of India.
 
• The commission was tasked with evaluating the state of education in India and recommending reforms to improve access to education.
 
• It placed strong emphasis on the expansion of primary education, especially among rural communities and underprivileged sections.
 
• It advocated for the involvement of local self-governments to fund and manage primary education institutions.
 
• The commission also recommended the establishment of secondary schools to cater to the growing demand for higher education.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Ripon:**

 
 
• Lord Ripon served as the Viceroy of India from **1880 to 1884**.
 
• He is known as the **Father of Local Self-Government in India** for his efforts in decentralizing administrative powers.
 
• Ripon implemented several reforms in education, local governance, and civil liberties.
 
 
 
• **Primary Education in Colonial India:**
 
 
• During the 19th century, education in India was limited to elite groups, while rural and underprivileged communities had minimal access.
 
• The Hunter Commission sought to address these disparities by promoting universal access to primary education.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Hunter Commission:**
 
 
• It marked a pivotal step in formalizing education policies in British India.
 
• The recommendations laid the groundwork for further education reforms in the 20th century.
 
 
 
• **Local Self-Government:**
 
 
• Ripon encouraged local self-governments to take responsibility for funding and managing schools.
 
• This approach empowered local bodies and improved accountability in education delivery.

questions.question: The concept of the Self-Help Group Bank Linkage Program was introduced by:
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Self-Help Group Bank Linkage Program (SHG-BLP)** was initiated by **NABARD** in 1992, marking a significant milestone in microfinance.
 
• The program aims to link **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**, typically formed by poor women, with banks to provide them access to formal financial services.
 
• It is considered the **world’s largest microfinance initiative**, with millions of SHGs formed and linked to banks across India.
 
• The program focuses on **empowering the rural poor** by providing them with financial resources to engage in income-generating activities.
 
• By 2023, it has helped **enhance financial inclusion** and enabled women in rural areas to improve their livelihoods and economic independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **What is NABARD?**

 
 
• **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)** is an apex development financial institution in India, established in **1982**.
 
• It focuses on **agriculture, rural development, and financial inclusion**.
 
• NABARD plays a key role in implementing and financing rural development schemes.
 
 
 
• **Self-Help Groups (SHGs):**
 
 
• SHGs are **informal groups of 10-20 people**, usually women, who come together to save and borrow money collectively.
 
• They promote **self-reliance and economic empowerment**.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of SHG-BLP:**
 
 
• Encourages savings among SHG members and links them to **formal banking institutions**.
 
• Provides **collateral-free loans** to members to support income-generating activities.
 
• Promotes group accountability and peer monitoring to ensure repayment.
 
 
 
• **Impact of SHG-BLP:**
 
 
• Enhanced **financial literacy** and inclusion in rural areas.
 
• Empowered women by increasing their participation in economic activities.
 
• Boosted rural entrepreneurship and poverty alleviation.

questions.question: Which famous monument of Vijayapura has a Whispering Gallery, where subtle sounds can be heard clearly even from a distance of 37 metres?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gol Gumbaz**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Gol Gumbaz**, located in Vijayapura (Bijapur), Karnataka, is renowned for its **Whispering Gallery**, where even the faintest sound echoes and can be heard clearly up to 37 meters away.
 
• It is the **mausoleum of Mohammed Adil Shah**, the Sultan of Bijapur, and was built in 1656.
 
• The structure is known for its **massive dome**, which is one of the largest unsupported domes in the world.
 
• The Whispering Gallery runs along the periphery of the dome and is an architectural wonder due to its acoustic properties.
 
• Gol Gumbaz is an iconic example of **Deccan Sultanate architecture**, showcasing Indo-Islamic design influences.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Architectural Features**:

 
 
• The Gol Gumbaz dome has a diameter of 44 meters, making it the second-largest pre-modern dome in the world.
 
• It is supported by eight intersecting arches and has no central pillar, which is a remarkable engineering feat.
 
 
 
• **Acoustics of the Whispering Gallery**:
 
 
• The gallery allows sound to travel across the dome, amplifying even the faintest whispers.
 
• This unique feature results from the dome's curvature and precise architectural design.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**:
 
 
• Mohammed Adil Shah commissioned the structure to serve as his final resting place.
 
• The monument reflects the grandeur and cultural advancements of the Deccan Sultanate.
 
 
 
• **Tourist Attraction**:
 
 
• Gol Gumbaz is one of the most visited historical sites in Karnataka, attracting tourists and architecture enthusiasts worldwide.
 
• The site also houses a museum showcasing artifacts from the Adil Shahi dynasty.

questions.question: __________ was an Indian mandolinist who was a master composer of the Carnatic style of classical music.

__
 
• Uppalapu Srinivas, popularly known as U. Srinivas, was a renowned **Indian mandolinist** and composer.
 
• He is credited with adapting the western mandolin to suit the **Carnatic style of classical music**.
 
• Srinivas performed his first major concert at the age of **9** during the Thyagaraja Aradhana festival at Kumbakonam.
 
• He was a recipient of prestigious awards like the **Padma Shri** in 1998 and the **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award** in 2009.
 
• Uppalapu Srinivas is often referred to as the **"Mandolin Maestro"** for his exceptional contribution to Indian classical music.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mandolin:**

 
 
• The mandolin is a stringed musical instrument in the lute family, typically played with a plectrum.
 
• It was originally a western instrument, but artists like U. Srinivas adapted it for Indian classical music.
 
 
 
• **Carnatic Music:**
 
 
• Carnatic music is a system of classical music associated with the southern part of India.
 
• It emphasizes vocal music and is characterized by intricate rhythmic patterns and improvisations.
 
 
 
• **Thyagaraja Aradhana:**
 
 
• An annual festival held in honor of Saint Thyagaraja, one of the greatest composers of Carnatic music.
 
• The event takes place in Thiruvaiyaru, Tamil Nadu, and attracts musicians and enthusiasts from around the world.
 
 
 
• **Notable Works of U. Srinivas:**
 
 
• Srinivas collaborated with global artists such as John McLaughlin and Michael Nyman, showcasing his versatility.
 
• He was part of the fusion group **Remember Shakti**, blending Indian classical with jazz.

questions.question: In which of the following dance performance is the main percussion instrument Edakka used?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mohiniattam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Edakka** is a prominent percussion instrument used in the classical dance form **Mohiniattam**, which originates from Kerala, India.
 
• The instrument produces soft and melodious sounds and is considered an essential part of the **musical accompaniment** for Mohiniattam performances.
 
• Mohiniattam is characterized by graceful movements, subtle expressions, and a repertoire that integrates **classical Carnatic music**.
 
• The **Edakka** is played with the hands, and its sound complements the lyrical and emotive nature of Mohiniattam.
 
• Other instruments like Veena, Mridangam, and Flute also accompany Mohiniattam performances, but the Edakka holds a unique place in its musical ensemble.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mohiniattam:**

 
 
• It is one of the eight classical dance forms of India, recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi.
 
• Mohiniattam translates to "Dance of the Enchantress" and is deeply rooted in the **Lasya** (feminine and graceful) aspect of classical dance.
 
• The dance form traditionally narrates stories from Hindu mythology, especially focusing on Lord Vishnu and his incarnations.
 
 
 
• **Edakka:**
 
 
• Also known as "Idakka," it is a traditional drum of Kerala used in temple rituals and classical music.
 
• Its construction involves a wooden drum with leather membranes, and it is known for its versatility in producing tonal variations.
 
• The Edakka is often associated with temple art forms like Kathakali and Mohiniattam.
 
 
 
• **Classical Dance Forms of India:**
 
 
• India has eight officially recognized classical dance forms: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Sattriya, and Mohiniattam.
 
• Each dance form has unique features, costumes, musical instruments, and regional significance.
 
 
 
• **Role of Music in Classical Dance:**
 
 
• Music plays a vital role in classical dance, helping to set the mood, rhythm, and narrative flow.
 
• Instruments like Mridangam, Veena, Flute, and Edakka are commonly used to complement the dancer's movements and expressions.

questions.question: What is the tenure of a Governor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The tenure of a Governor in India is **5 years**, as per Article 156 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Governor holds office **at the pleasure of the President** and may resign before completing their tenure.
 
• The 5-year term is counted from the date they take the **oath of office**.
 
• Governors can be reappointed or transferred to other states, and they may **continue in office even after their term ends** until a successor is appointed.
 
• Although the term is 5 years, the President has the authority to **remove a Governor** before the completion of their term without any justification.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 153:** There shall be a Governor for each state in India; however, one person can act as the Governor for two or more states.
 
• **Appointment:** The Governor is appointed by the President of India and is considered the constitutional head of the state.
 
• **Oath of Office:** The Governor takes an oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned state or the senior-most judge available.
 
• **Eligibility:** To be appointed as a Governor, a person must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years of age, and should not hold any office of profit.
 
• **Role:** The Governor acts as the link between the state government and the central government and plays a crucial role in the administration of the state under the provisions of the Constitution.

• **Vikram Chola's lineage:** Vikram Chola, a notable ruler of the Chola dynasty, was a descendant of both the Cholas and the Eastern Chalukyas, showcasing the dynastic alliances of the period.
 
• **Gangaikonda Chola:** Rajendra I Chola earned the title "Gangaikonda Chola" after his victorious expedition to the Ganges River, symbolizing his expansionist policies.
 
• The Cholas were known for their contributions to art, architecture, and administration, with temples like the Brihadeeswarar Temple standing as a testament to their legacy.
 
• The Chola dynasty played a significant role in maritime trade and had extensive influence in Southeast Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Temple Architecture:** The Cholas are renowned for their monumental temple architecture, especially the Brihadeeswarar Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• **Naval Power:** The Chola Empire had a powerful navy, enabling them to establish trade and cultural ties with Southeast Asia, including the Srivijaya Empire.
 
• **Literary Contributions:** The Chola period saw significant advancements in Tamil literature, with works like Kamba Ramayanam being composed during their reign.
 
• **Gangaikonda Cholapuram:** Rajendra I established Gangaikonda Cholapuram as a new capital to commemorate his conquests and to signify the Chola Empire's dominance.

questions.question: Which of the following sessions of the Indian National Congress was headed by Sarojini Naidu?

• During her tenure as the Congress president, Sarojini Naidu emphasized the importance of communal harmony and national unity.

questions.question: Which local storm is also known as 'Kalbaisakhi'?

__
 
• **Nor Westers** are locally known as **'Kalbaisakhi'** in West Bengal and parts of Eastern India.
 
• These storms occur predominantly during the **pre-monsoon season**, typically from March to May.
 
• Nor Westers are characterized by **sudden, violent thunderstorms** accompanied by heavy rain and strong winds.
 
• These storms are particularly beneficial for agriculture as they help in **irrigating crops like mango, jute, and rice**.
 
• They are most common in areas such as **West Bengal, Assam, Odisha, and Jharkhand**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Formation of Nor Westers:**

 
 
• Nor Westers are caused by the interaction of warm, moist air from the Bay of Bengal and cool, dry air from northern India.
 
• The instability in the atmosphere leads to the formation of cumulonimbus clouds, resulting in thunderstorms.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Mango Cultivation:**
 
 
• Nor Westers are referred to as 'Mango Showers' in other parts of India as they aid in the ripening of mangoes.
 
• The rains from these storms are crucial for improving fruit quality and yield.
 
 
 
• **Associated Weather Phenomena:**
 
 
• These storms can cause hail, which sometimes damages crops and property.
 
• High winds and lightning are common features of Nor Westers, occasionally leading to fatalities and infrastructural damage.
 
 
 
• **Regional Names:**
 
 
• In West Bengal and Assam, they are called 'Kalbaisakhi,' meaning 'Calamity of the Month of Vaisakh.'
 
• In Kerala and coastal Karnataka, similar pre-monsoon rains are referred to as 'Mango Showers.'

questions.question: Which substance is commonly added to tap water to make it safe for drinking by killing harmful microorganisms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chlorine**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Chlorine is widely used to disinfect water as it is highly effective in killing bacteria, viruses, and other harmful microorganisms.
 
• Water chlorination is a common practice in municipal water treatment plants worldwide to ensure drinking water is safe.
 
• Chlorine works by breaking down the cell walls of microorganisms, thereby inactivating or destroying them.
 
• In addition to disinfection, chlorine also helps to control algae and remove unpleasant tastes and odors caused by organic compounds in water.
 
• The World Health Organization (WHO) recognizes chlorination as a key method for improving drinking water safety globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Free Chlorine:**

 
 
• This refers to the chlorine available in water to disinfect, which includes hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ions (OCl-).
 
• The recommended level of free chlorine in drinking water is 0.2–0.5 mg/L to ensure effective disinfection.
 
 
 
• **Chlorination Byproducts:**
 
 
• When chlorine reacts with natural organic matter in water, it can form byproducts such as trihalomethanes (THMs).
 
• While these byproducts are monitored, the risk they pose is much lower than the risk of consuming untreated water.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Disinfection Methods:**
 
 
• Other methods like ozone treatment and UV radiation are also used for water disinfection, but chlorination remains the most economical and widely used.
 
 
 
• **History of Chlorination:**
 
 
• Water chlorination was first introduced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to combat waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid.
 
• The first continuous chlorination of public water supplies was in Jersey City, New Jersey, in 1908.
 
 
 
• **Health Benefits:**
 
 
• Chlorinated water significantly reduces the prevalence of waterborne diseases such as diarrhea, dysentery, and hepatitis A.
 
• It plays a critical role in achieving public health goals related to safe drinking water.

questions.question: Why will a person weigh more at the north or south pole?

options.text: Due to Earth’s distance from the sun
Due to variation in centrifugal force of earth with latitude
Due to variation in centripetal force of earth with altitude
Due to variation in centripetal force of earth with latitude

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Due to variation in centrifugal force of earth with latitude**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The centrifugal force on Earth is caused by its rotation and is strongest at the equator due to the higher rotational velocity.
 
• At the poles, the centrifugal force is negligible as the poles do not experience the same rotational velocity as the equator.
 
• Less centrifugal force at the poles reduces the outward "push," causing a person to weigh more compared to their weight at the equator.
 
• Earth’s shape, which is slightly oblate (flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator), also contributes to the variation in weight.
 
• The gravitational force is slightly stronger at the poles due to the reduced distance from the Earth’s center compared to the equator.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Centrifugal Force:** A pseudo-force that acts outward on a mass when it is rotating, proportional to the rotational velocity and the radius of rotation.
 
• **Earth’s Shape:** The Earth is an oblate spheroid; it is flatter at the poles and bulges at the equator, influencing gravity and centrifugal forces.
 
• ** Gravity is slightly stronger at the poles because they are closer to the Earth’s center compared to the equator.
 
• Weight vs Mass:** Weight is the force exerted due to gravity and varies with location, while mass remains constant regardless of location.
 
• **Rotational Impact:** Earth’s rotation affects the distribution of centrifugal force, which contributes to the difference in apparent weight across latitudes.

questions.question: For most of the ecosystem, what is the primary source of energy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sunlight**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sunlight** is the primary source of energy for most ecosystems as it drives the process of **photosynthesis**, enabling plants to produce food. 
 
• Through photosynthesis, plants convert sunlight into chemical energy, which becomes the foundation for the food chain in ecosystems.
 
• Sunlight provides energy directly to producers (plants, algae, cyanobacteria), which are then consumed by herbivores and higher-level consumers.
 
• Solar energy also influences critical environmental factors, such as temperature and climate, which directly impact ecosystems.
 
• Without sunlight, ecosystems would collapse as the flow of energy through trophic levels would cease to function.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Photosynthesis:** A biochemical process in which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water to produce glucose and oxygen. 
 
• **Energy Flow in Ecosystems:** The transfer of energy begins with producers (plants) and moves through consumers (herbivores, carnivores) and decomposers (fungi, bacteria). 
 
• **Autotrophs:** Organisms like plants and algae that produce their own food using sunlight are known as autotrophs or primary producers.
 
• **Trophic Levels:** Each level in a food chain represents a trophic level, starting with producers, followed by primary consumers, secondary consumers, and tertiary consumers. 
 
• **Solar Radiation:** Nearly 70% of solar energy reaching Earth is absorbed by the atmosphere, land, and oceans, while the rest is reflected back into space.

questions.question: In which of the following types of regions, is the maximum temperature variation observed between a day and the same night?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Desert**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Deserts** experience the maximum temperature variation between day and night due to the lack of vegetation and moisture in the soil, resulting in rapid heating and cooling.
 
• During the day, deserts receive intense solar radiation, causing temperatures to soar to extreme levels.
 
• At night, the absence of clouds and moisture leads to rapid loss of heat through radiation, causing the temperature to drop significantly.
 
• The temperature difference between day and night in desert regions can be as high as 20°C to 30°C.
 
• Examples of deserts with high diurnal temperature variations include the Sahara Desert, Thar Desert, and the Mojave Desert.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Diurnal Temperature Variation:**

 
 
• It refers to the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures within a single day.
 
• Regions with dry air and minimal vegetation, such as deserts, exhibit the highest diurnal temperature variations.
 
 
 
• **Role of Vegetation and Moisture:**
 
 
• Vegetation and moisture act as insulators, moderating the temperature variation by absorbing heat during the day and releasing it at night.
 
• Lack of these factors in deserts leads to extremes in temperature changes.
 
 
 
• **Heat Radiation Process:**
 
 
• During the night, heat from the surface radiates back into the atmosphere, leading to rapid cooling in regions like deserts.
 
• Cloud cover and humidity slow down this process in other regions, reducing temperature variation.
 
 
 
• **Comparison to Coastal Areas:**
 
 
• Coastal regions exhibit minimal temperature variation between day and night due to the moderating effect of nearby water bodies.
 
• Water has a high heat capacity, absorbing and releasing heat slowly, stabilizing the temperature.
